context: In the figure, f(k) corresponds to fib(k) in the code. The base cases are f(1) = 0 and f(2) = 1. For k > 2, the function computes f(k−1) + f(k−2).
description: The figure expands only the first few levels and leaves the total depth unspecified. For small n, some branches reach f(1) or f(2) early and stop before reaching all the levels shown symbolically.

frames.explanation: Each call f(k) that has yet to reach a base case makes a left call f(k−1) and a right call f(k−2). For example, the root's right call f(n−2) at level 2 and the call f(n−2) on the left side of level 3 lie on different paths. Each computes its own result without automatically merging the calls or reusing the result.
frames.title: Fibonacci recursion tree

result: Branches stop at a base case, so the number of calls does not double at every level. Even so, repeated expansion makes the number of calls grow exponentially with n. Counting the root as level 1, the longest chain of calls in the code has n−1 levels for n ≥ 2 (only 2 levels for n = 3). For n = 1, the root is the only level. The n levels mentioned in the text describe linear growth in depth, rather than an exact count.
summary: Branches of the recursion solve the same subproblems repeatedly, which explains why naive recursion does so much work.

tables.caption: Calls at each level, with repeated names denoting separate calls
rows: Two ellipses branch from each node in the preceding level. The individual calls are omitted.
